1. Scientific Analysis

Analysis Type

Row-median AFM leveling + square-pixel calibration + targeted Fourier reflection mapping (fourier_reflection_map) of mica lattice/adsorbate periodicity

Interpretation

The AFM height map of mica in 2 mM KCl was leveled (row-median) and analyzed by targeted Fourier reflection mapping on calibrated square pixels (0.0294 nm/px, 15.03 nm field of view). The dominant periodicity is a reflection at d = 0.485 nm with high statistical significance (sigma = 7.3), accompanied by a nearly equally strong reflection at d = 0.429 nm (sigma = 7.05). Both correspond to atomic-scale lateral spacings in the ~0.4–0.5 nm range, consistent with the pseudo-hexagonal ditrigonal cavity lattice of the mica (001) basal plane and/or an ordered hydration/adsorbate layer templated by it. Notably, the 0.485 nm value is ~7% smaller than the nominal mica basal spacing of 0.52 nm; this shortfall exceeds the ~2% pixel/calibration resolution and may reflect residual lateral scanner calibration error, thermal drift, or that the resolved periodicity is not the bare mica lattice but a commensurate adsorbate/ion-hydration superlattice with a slightly compressed repeat. The presence of two comparably strong reflections (0.485 and 0.429 nm) rather than a single spacing is consistent with the two-dimensional oblique/hexagonal lattice producing multiple in-plane periodicities (e.g., along different lattice directions) rather than a single 1D fringe. No genuine superstructure or satellite reflections were resolved (the apparent 1.00 nm 'satellite candidate' has negative sigma and is a harmonic artifact, not a real feature), indicating no long-range reconstruction or ordered ion superlattice at this resolution. The band-amplitude map is homogeneous (CV = 0.11) with only a smooth low-frequency intensity gradient (bright lobe at right), which is topographic in origin rather than a distinct ordered domain; consistently, the ordered-domain mask returns domain_fraction = 0.0 and localized_ordering_confirmed = false. Together this indicates the periodic order is spatially pervasive (not confined to isolated patches) across the imaged area, i.e., a single continuous lattice/adsorbate film rather than segregated ordered domains. The spot SNR comparison (417 domain vs 263 bulk) does not reach the threshold for localized enhancement, reinforcing that ordering is uniform.

3. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: The mica (001) surface in 2 mM KCl exhibits a spatially pervasive, homogeneous in-plane periodic lattice with a dominant spacing of d = 0.485 nm (sigma = 7.3), ~7% smaller than the nominal 0.52 nm mica basal spacing, with no resolvable superstructure or ordered ion superlattice.

Scientific Impact: Distinguishing the bare mica basal lattice from a hydration/ion-templated adsorbate layer is central to understanding electrical-double-layer and ion-adsorption structure at charged mineral-water interfaces; the ~7% compressed repeat and absence of a superstructure constrain whether adsorbed K+/hydration layers form commensurate ordered arrays or remain lattice-fluid at this ionic strength.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone observed a ~0.485 nm in-plane periodicity (compressed relative to the 0.52 nm mica basal spacing) on mica under dilute KCl, and is this the bare lattice or an ion/hydration-templated layer?

Keywords: mica basal plane, AFM, KCl electrolyte, Fourier lattice spacing, electrical double layer, ion hydration

4. Caveats & Limitations

The 0.485 nm spacing is ~7% below the accepted 0.52 nm mica basal spacing — beyond the ~2% pixel calibration — so absolute lattice assignment is uncertain and may reflect residual lateral scanner calibration/drift error; independent calibration on a known standard is needed. A second strong reflection at 0.429 nm (sigma = 7.05) is not fully interpreted and may represent a second lattice direction or an adsorbate periodicity. The 1.00 nm 'satellite candidate' has negative sigma and is a Fourier harmonic artifact, not a real superstructure. The ordered-domain mask (frac = 0.00) is uninformative here because ordering is uniform rather than patchy; its null result should not be read as absence of periodicity given the clearly significant sigma~7 reflection. Analysis cannot distinguish the bare mica lattice from a commensurate adsorbate/hydration layer sharing the same registry.
